posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
"Wannabe home holographers can get a taste of the technology's maddening limitations by purchasing the do-it-yourself, $99 Litiholo kit.'

We await the Great Day of a pic of a Liti hologram so that the "maddening limitations" of the technology may live up to the maddening marketing. 

Actually, another point is that they don't seem to have realised that you can make a hologram from a video sequence. We have a hologram of Q (from Star Trek) waving at you from the plate, by ABNH. The Michael Jordan holo was taken from a video sequence, it's not a pulse poirttrait.They've also missed out on the MIT concept of the holo-video using an acousto-optic crystal. I saw a demo of this in around 1990 which was pretty small. It was a (old version) Star Ship Enterprise slowly revolving in space from a crystal only about an inch square. Mitch later told me they'd scaled it up to 4x5.

posts.author: edelbrp
posts.content_md:
> **Dinesh:** "Wannabe home holographers can get a taste of the technology's maddening limitations by purchasing the do-it-yourself, $99 Litiholo kit.'

Ouch, yeah I read that too. Liti has had a lot of press lately. Hopefully it will give them enough to get them going and perfect their technology.

In general the article didn't seem all that informed, but does touch on some of the elements of what it takes to make a technology be marketable for entertainment.

Small monochromatic holograms of small-dead-things isn't all that fun for most folks. A holodeck is (but not yet feasible, of course).

Funny, many of the /. comments ventured into the p0rn uses of holography entertainment. (whoa! check out the 3D on THAT!) 

-Phil
